lesson.title: One Package, Many Hops: How Packets Cross the Internet
lesson.summary: A packet is the network-layer unit of data, most commonly an IP packet, that carries a source and destination address across multiple interconnected networks, getting rewrapped in a fresh frame at every hop along the way.
lesson.body:
A frame, from the previous chapter, only makes sense across a single physical link between two directly connected devices. Getting data from your laptop to a server on the other side of the world requires crossing many such links in sequence, through routers that each connect different networks together, and that is the job of a packet. A packet is the unit of data at the network layer, most commonly an IP packet, and it consists of a header, holding a source address, a destination address, and other control information, wrapped around a payload, all of it built to be routed across an unbroken chain of networks rather than just one local segment.

The IPv4 header shows what that control information actually looks like in bytes. Its standard, fixed portion is 20 bytes, extendable up to 60 bytes if optional fields are present, and it includes a 4-byte source address and a 4-byte destination address, a 1-byte Time to Live field, and a 1-byte protocol field identifying what kind of data the packet is carrying, for instance the value 6 for TCP or 17 for UDP. The Time to Live field, usually called TTL, is decremented by one at every router the packet passes through, and if it ever reaches zero the packet is discarded rather than forwarded again, which prevents a misconfigured network from letting a packet loop forever. IPv6, the newer version of the protocol, uses a different but conceptually similar fixed 40-byte header.

Here is where the connection to frames becomes concrete. Suppose your laptop sends a request to a web server three router hops away. The first hop is your laptop to your home Wi-Fi router, and the IP packet travels across it wrapped inside an 802.11 Wi-Fi frame. Your router then forwards the same packet onward across your ISP's network, but now it is wrapped inside a completely different frame, likely an Ethernet frame, appropriate for that next physical link. This repeats at every router along the path: the packet is unwrapped from the frame that carried it across the previous hop and rewrapped in a brand new frame suited to the next one. The packet's IP header stays essentially unchanged end to end, aside from the TTL field ticking down by one at each hop, even though the frame around it is completely replaced every single time.

This design, called packet switching, is a foundational choice in how the internet works, and it is worth contrasting with the alternative. Rather than reserving a dedicated path for one conversation the way a traditional phone circuit does, packets from many completely unrelated conversations are interleaved on the same shared links, and each packet is routed independently based on its own destination address. This lets the network use its capacity far more efficiently, since idle moments in one conversation can be filled with another conversation's packets, at the cost of no individual packet being guaranteed a fixed delivery time.

Every field discussed in this chapter, the 20-byte header, the 4-byte addresses, the single-byte TTL, is measured in the bytes introduced two chapters ago, and the packet as a whole sits directly above frames in the stack, carried by a fresh one at every hop. The next two chapters look at what typically rides inside a packet's payload: the transport-layer units called segments and datagrams.
